newsitem.title: USA: Budget pact seen as initial positive for US bonds.
newsitem.headline: Budget pact seen as initial positive for US bonds.

text.p: After ignoring all rhetoric on a balanced budget accord for the the first four months of 1997, the U.S. Treasury market has finally taken notice and started reacting positively to hints that a deal is imminent.
But even as the market begins to sense an agreement is within reach -- perhaps as early as Thursday afternoon -- observers fear that many players are getting ahead of themselves.
Analysts said any budget pact would provide an initial boost to the market.
But they do not expect a lasting or overwhelmingly positive impact unless legislators surprise them with a serious deficit-cutting package -- something which the market believes is unlikely.

Analysts said that first and foremost, the market just wants a deal that balances the budget by 2002. "That would be viewed as progress as far as the market is concerned," said Brian Wesbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc.
However, the market would frown at a back-loaded deal which delayed major spending cuts until after the year 2000.
Bond market players would prefer a capital gains tax cut and a slower pace of government spending in the early years.
"The only way (a budget deal) would be negative for the market is if spending cuts are back-loaded and if there are no serious tax cuts that would boost savings and investments," Wesbury said.

Comments from administration and congressional leaders on the near-term probability of an agreement to balance the budget by 2002 have played a role in the Treasury market's rally this week. Yields have fallen to lows not seen since before the Federal Reserve raised rates in March.

"It's starting to creep in as a supporting influence; there's no doubt about it," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "But the bulk (of the rally) has been on the improving economic backdrop. In the long run, fiscal policy is a secondary influence on money markets."

But that does not mean the market won't rejoice when a budget agreement finally comes, analysts said. Whether the budget is viewed at first as credible or not, a deal should help the market since it represents short-term momentum and cooperation between Democrats and Republicans, players said.

Therefore, "when we get a deal, we'll see a continuation of the technical rally," said Neil DeSarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. He questioned, however, whether the market was setting itself up for an eventual letdown.

For the past couple days, despite some grumbling from Congressional Democrats, most of those involved in the budget talks have expressed optimism that an accord could be reached by the time President Clinton leaves for his Mexico trip on Tuesday, with some saying a deal could happen by the weekend.

"The big parameters are about to be settled I think. The devil, however, still is in the details and that's particularly true of tax cuts," Rep. John Spratt of South Carolina, a ranking Democrat on the House of Representatives Budget Committee, said on Thursday.
Spratt's comments followed those of Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who on Wednesday night said talks with the White House have gotten "much closer" to an agreement.
Even Clinton hinted that the broad outlines of a balanced budget agreement may be taking shape.

That optimism seemed to please the bond market. There had been unsubstantiated rumors on Thursday morning that an agreement had been reached, cited as the main reason Treasury prices started climibing. Likewise, when word spread that a deal was not as imminent as the market had thought, Treasury prices edged back down.

Yet, market participants recall a time back in late 1995 and early 1996 when the market was sure a budget agreement would occur. A massive rally ensued, as the market figured the Fed would follow a budget deal with lowering interest rates.
When a deal could not be reached, even after a bitter fight between Democrats and Republicans in which the government was shut down twice, the market sold off.
So, what is different now?

"Certainly the way they are going about it is different than 1995," said Greg Jones, chief economist at Briefing.com, an Internet-based fixed income service. "This time, there are discussions. Last time around it was Republicans seeing if they could shove a budget down Clinton's throat."
Plus, Jones noted, the two sides have less work to do this time to cut a deficit that is expected to be about $70 to $90 billion this year, down from $107 billion in 1996 and $164 billion in 1995.
"Net net, the job is easier," he said.
Even so, both sides still have to get past the hurdle of how to agree on Medicare and taxes, the main sticking points.
Even if there is a compromise on those points and a agreement is reached soon, much work will still be needed since the deal will have to be approved by the House, Senate and White House.
"I assume that at this point, even if they had a deal in the next five minutes, the market will react positively," Jones said, "but after that, the market would look at it and see not much is there."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
